newsitem.title: USA: Researchers develop warmer cotton but a ways to go.
newsitem.headline: Researchers develop warmer cotton but a ways to go.

text.p: Scientists with the Agracetus biotechnology firm announced the development of a gene-altered cotton plant with better insulating fibres, but said the new, warmer cotton is years away from being sold to consumers.

Researchers at the Monsanto Co unit said on Tuesday the development represents an important breakthrough in the genetic engineering of cotton plants, since the cotton was given its new traits via foreign genes -- a process not possible through normal crop breeding.

"What we wanted to try and do was to take genes and see if this ... would give the cotton any new characteristics," said researcher and molecular biologist Greg Keller. "We've demonstrated this can be done."

A spokesman for Monsanto, which this year offered two big genetically modified products to farmers -- its controversial so-called Roundup Ready soybeans and its Bollguard cotton -- said the new cotton variety reflects the type of biogenetic research underway. Realistically the product is at least 10 years away from commercialisation, however.

"Anything that they're doing is at least a decade away from commercialisation," said Gary Burton of St Louis-based Monsanto. "The things that we're going to commercialise in 2001 are already being grown in greenhouses."
The new cotton has been shown to hold 12 percent more heat than regular cotton cloth, and retain heat longer.

The new insulating qualities of the cotton were attained by giving the cotton, through a gene-delivery technique known as particle bombardment, the ability to make a natural plastic called polyhydroxybutyrate or PHB. PHB resembles polypropylene, a synthetic material used in making thermal clothing.
The PHB genes were obtained from a soil bacterium that creates the chemical as an energy source.
Researcher Keller said the current challenge now is to find a way for the cotton to produce more PHB to increase its heat-retaining ability.
"It will probably take three to five years to see if we can actually produce enough (PHB) to get the characteristics we want," said Keller.

Monsanto has been weathering a storm of recent criticism the past several weeks over its new genetically modified soybeans, which were grown commercially by U.S. farmers for the first time this year. Some U.S. and European consumer activists have raised sharp objections to the new product, saying it could pose health risks and harm the environment.
Monsanto's Barton shrugged off the criticism. "It goes with leadership and being first on the market. It's a case of reacting without understanding the product's real benefits," he said.
